_comment: Theme taxonomy for the Owen/Stott/Lennox corpus. Does NOT redefine the 3 pre-existing keys (atonement_models, corporate_headship, image_of_god) so their Heiser/Bradley/synthesis descriptions are preserved. parent_theme values may point to those existing keys or to keys defined below.

themes.description: Christ bore in the sinner's place the penalty due to sin, satisfying God's holy justice. Affirmed by Owen and Stott as a true juridical facet of the cross (held within, not against, the wider representation frame).

The cross as the God-provided satisfaction of God's own holy wrath against sin — not the pagan appeasement of a reluctant deity. Stott's defence of 'propitiation' against a merely 'expiation' reading.

Particular redemption: Christ's death actually and effectually secured the salvation of a definite people rather than making salvation a bare possibility for all. Owen's central thesis (a distinctly Reformed position).
key_works: Owen, The Death of Death in the Death of Christ

themes.description: Salvation as liberation from bondage purchased at the price of Christ's blood — the marketplace and slave-yard image (lytron).
The eternal compact of Father, Son, and Spirit to save a people, grounding the unity and definiteness of Christ's saving work.
Why the death of Christ stands at the centre of the gospel and of Jesus' own self-understanding.
The atonement as God's initiative ending the enmity between God and sinners, and between estranged peoples, making one new humanity.
The forensic declaration that the ungodly are counted righteous on the ground of Christ's imputed righteousness, received through faith alone — the 'great exchange', not infused righteousness.
key_works: Owen, The Doctrine of Justification by Faith

themes.description: The role and limits of the law — its inability to justify, its work as a guardian leading to Christ, and the believer's relation to it under grace.
Believers brought from slavery into the family of God as sons and heirs, receiving the Spirit of the Son.
God's holy, settled opposition to sin — the backdrop against which propitiation and the gospel are rightly understood.
The fact and nature of sin as universal self-centredness that separates humanity from God.
The believer's incorporation into Christ — dead and risen with him — as the spine of salvation and the root of communion, assurance, and sanctification.
Owen's teaching that believers hold distinct fellowship with each divine Person — the Father chiefly in love, the Son in grace, the Spirit in comfort.

themes.theme_label: The Work of the Holy Spirit
themes.description: The person and work of the Holy Spirit — regeneration, indwelling, filling, comfort, assurance, and the fruit he produces. Includes Stott's baptism-vs-fullness argument.
The Spirit's lifelong work of conforming believers to Christ, and the believer's active pursuit of holiness.
The believer's daily, Spirit-empowered killing of indwelling sin — 'be killing sin or it will be killing you' (Romans 8:13).
key_works: Owen, Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers

themes.description: The nature, deceit, and prevailing power of the sin that remains in believers (Romans 7).
key_works: Owen, The Nature and Power of Indwelling Sin

themes.description: The preservation and persevering of believers, and the biblical warnings that serve as a means to it.
The grounds and experience of Christian assurance — resting on Christ, the Spirit's witness, and God's unbreakable love.
The glory of Christ's person (the two natures united in one), his mediatorial offices, and the transforming power of beholding him by faith.
key_works: Owen, Meditations on the Glory of Christ

themes.description: The divine claims and identity of Jesus — his self-witness and the corroborating evidence of his character and resurrection.
Christ as the merciful, faithful, and eternal high priest after the order of Melchizedek, ever living to intercede (Hebrews).
The better covenant enacted on better promises, mediated by Christ and fulfilling and surpassing the old (Hebrews 8).

themes.theme_label: The Sabbath Rest of the Gospel
themes.description: The promised rest that remains for the people of God, entered now by faith and consummated hereafter (Hebrews 4).

Reading Genesis 1 faithfully — God as Creator who speaks the world into being — without making secondary questions (the earth's age, the length of the days) a test of orthodoxy. Lennox's science-and-Scripture approach.
key_works: Lennox, Seven Days That Divide the World

themes.description: God's sovereign superintendence of all things, working even through human evil and suffering for good (Joseph; Daniel).

How God's sovereignty and genuine human freedom and responsibility are held together in Scripture. Lennox's eirenic challenge to strict theological determinism — in deliberate dialogue with the Reformed tradition (Owen).
How faith reckons with suffering and evil under a good and sovereign God.
The distinctive ethics of the kingdom — the Christian counter-culture of the Sermon on the Mount and the transformed life under the cross.
key_works: Stott, The Message of the Sermon on the Mount

themes.description: Following Christ in wholehearted, costly obedience and daily devotion.
Prayer offered for God's eyes rather than human applause, shaped by the pattern of the Lord's Prayer.

themes.theme_label: Faithful Witness in a Hostile Culture
themes.description: Living with integrity and courage as a believing minority inside a pagan or secular superpower (Daniel).
Discerning truth amid cultural pressure, and distinguishing Scripture itself from our interpretations of it.
The summons to repentance, faith, and open commitment to Christ, and the response the gospel demands.
The hope of resurrection and the everlasting kingdom given to the Son of Man.
Christ's resurrection as God's public vindication of his person and claims.
The one new humanity in Christ — Jew and Gentile — and the unity and gifts that build up the body.
Marriage as the earthly picture of the union between Christ and his church (Ephesians 5).
The believer's stand against the unseen powers, clothed in the armour of God (Ephesians 6).
The new creation inaugurated in Christ, in which what counts is not religious markers but transformation (Galatians 6:15).
